context: linear network · deep excavation, laid from the outfall upstream, air / water tests & CCTV survey

brief.intro: New to this project type? A sewerage network collects wastewater from every plot and carries it to a pumping station or treatment plant. Most of it flows by gravity, so every pipe must fall at an exact gradient — which makes sewers the deepest utility in the road, and the first one built. Work starts at the lowest point (the outfall or pumping station) and proceeds upstream, manhole to manhole, so each new length can drain. Where gravity cannot do the job, a lift or pumping station pushes the flow through a pressurised rising main. Deep trenches mean shoring, dewatering and slow progress, and each length must pass a leakage test and a CCTV inspection before the road is closed above it.

scope.name: Survey, levels & existing services
scope.desc: Accurate levels are essential — the whole design depends on gradient.

scope.name: Deep excavation, shoring & dewatering
scope.desc: Trenches several metres deep, supported and kept dry while pipe is laid.

scope.name: Gravity sewer pipes
scope.desc: uPVC, GRP, vitrified clay or concrete pipes laid to line and gradient between manholes.

scope.name: Manholes & inspection chambers
scope.desc: Precast or cast-in-situ manholes at every change of direction, level or diameter.

scope.name: House connections
scope.desc: Branch connections from each plot to the sewer, with an inspection chamber at the boundary.

scope.name: Lift / pumping stations
scope.desc: Wet well, pumps, valves, power and controls where the flow must be lifted.

scope.name: Rising (force) mains
scope.desc: Pressure pipe from the pumping station to the discharge point.

scope.name: Trenchless crossings
scope.desc: Micro-tunnelling or pipe jacking under main roads, railways and canals.

scope.name: Testing & CCTV
scope.desc: Air or water leakage tests, mandrel test and CCTV survey of every length.

scope.name: Backfill & reinstatement
scope.desc: Compacted backfill in layers and reinstatement of the road above.

scope.name: Connection to the existing system
scope.desc: Breaking into the existing sewer or treatment-works inlet, with flow diversion.

glossary.plain: a pipe that flows part-full, driven only by its slope.
the level of the inside bottom of the pipe — the number the gradient is set out from.
a chamber giving access to the sewer; placed at every bend, junction and change of gradient.
a pressurised pipe that carries pumped sewage uphill.
a small pumping station that raises sewage so it can flow by gravity again.
installing the pipe by pushing it through the ground from a shaft, without an open trench.
pumping groundwater down so the trench is dry enough to lay pipe.
a leakage test on a length of sewer between two manholes.
a camera run through the finished pipe to prove it is clean, aligned and undamaged.
temporarily pumping the existing flow around the point where the new sewer is connected.

must_get_right: Build from the downstream end upward. A sewer laid in the middle of the route with nowhere to drain cannot be tested or used, and the levels cannot be corrected later.
Sewers go in before every other utility because they are deepest — the sewer programme sets the start date of water, power and telecom in the same road.
Deep-trench production is slow and depends on shoring and dewatering; plan it as metres per day by depth band, not as one rate for the whole network.
The pumping station is a long job in its own right (deep wet well, pumps, power supply). Start it early — the network cannot be commissioned until it works.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities are organised by sewer run (manhole to manhole) grouped by catchment, in the order of construction from the outfall upstream, so the completed and tested length is always a connected, drainable system.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Standard site calendar for pipe laying; dewatering runs continuously (24 hours, 7 days) once started. Connection to the live system is done at low-flow hours (night) on its own calendar.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving chain is: pumping-station structure and outfall → trunk sewer upstream from the outfall → laterals → house connections, with each run following dewater → excavate → lay → test → backfill. In parallel the pumping station is fitted out and powered. The network is commissioned only when sewers are CCTV-accepted, the station is wet-tested and the rising main is pressure-tested.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Ground and groundwater are as in the soil report; permits are granted in construction order (downstream first); power supply to the pumping station is available on the assumed date; the receiving sewer or treatment works can accept the flow at handover.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: The schedule tracks the following as milestones because they drive the programme:

rows: Large-diameter GRP / concrete pipe & precast manholes

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Trench depth limits output and needs shoring; the open length is limited in public roads; dewatering discharge needs a permit and a discharge point. Deep manholes and the wet well are confined spaces.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Main risks: higher groundwater or rock than expected, collapse or settlement next to deep trenches, level errors found at CCTV stage, late power supply to the pumping station, and late pump delivery. Contingency is held on the deep trunk sewer and before the station commissioning.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 by sewer run and catchment; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the excavation, pipe-laying and manhole crews — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
